en: Paṭisambhidāmagga 2,
Yuganaddhavagga 2.5.
Discourse on Dispassion (Virāgakathā)
Dispassion is the path; liberation is the fruit.
How is dispassion the path?

At the moment of the stream-entry path, right view—in the sense of seeing—is dispassionate toward wrong view; it is dispassionate toward the defilements that follow upon it and toward the aggregates; and it is dispassionate toward all external signs.
Dispassion has dispassion as its object, dispassion as its domain; it has arisen in dispassion, is established in dispassion, and is grounded in dispassion.

Regarding "dispassion": there are two kinds of dispassion—the Nibbāna that is dispassion, and all those states born of having Nibbāna as their object which are also dispassion. Thus, they are "dispassions."
The seven factors that arise together proceed toward dispassion; thus, it is "the path of dispassion.
By means of this path, the Buddhas and their disciples go to Nibbāna, the direction not yet gone to;
thus, it is "the eightfold path."

"Of all the paths belonging to the various sects of ascetics and brahmins, this Noble Eightfold Path alone is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent"— thus, among paths,
the eightfold is the best. In the sense of directing [the mind], right intention is free from wrong intention.
In the sense of embracing, right speech is disjoined from wrong speech.
In the sense of origination, right action is disjoined from wrong action.
In the sense of purification, right livelihood is disjoined from wrong livelihood.
In the sense of exertion, right effort is detached from wrong effort.
In the sense of establishing, right mindfulness is detached from wrong mindfulness.
In the sense of non-distraction, right concentration is detached from wrong concentration.
One becomes dispassionate toward the defilements that follow after it and toward the aggregates;
one becomes dispassionate toward all external signs.
This dispassion has dispassion as its object, dispassion as its domain, has arisen in dispassion, is established in dispassion, and is grounded in dispassion.
Dispassion (*virāga*):
there are two kinds of dispassion—the dispassion that is Nibbāna itself, and all those states born of having Nibbāna as their object; these are "dispassions.
Because the seven co-nascent factors proceed toward dispassion, it is called the "path of dispassion" (*virāgo maggo*).
By this path, both Buddhas and their disciples go to the direction they have not yet gone— the Nibbāna— thus it is the Eightfold Path.
Among all the paths of the various ascetics and brahmins, those of other doctrines, this very Noble Eightfold Path is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent.
Of paths, the eightfold path is supreme.

At the moment of the once-returning path, right view in the sense of seeing … [and so on] … right concentration in the sense of non-distraction abandons the gross fetters of sensual lust and ill will, and the gross underlying tendencies of sensual lust … [and so on] … [as appropriate].
One becomes dispassionate toward the underlying tendency to aversion; one becomes dispassionate toward the defilements that follow upon it and toward the aggregates;
and one becomes dispassionate toward all external signs.
Dispassion has dispassion as its object, dispassion as its domain; it is fully manifested in dispassion, established in dispassion, and grounded in dispassion.
Dispassion: there are two kinds of dispassion—the dispassion that is Nibbāna, and all those states born of having Nibbāna as their object are also dispassion;
thus they are "dispassions. The seven factors born together with it proceed toward dispassion; thus it is the "path of dispassion."
By this path, both Buddhas and their disciples go to the direction they have not yet gone—the Nibbāna;
thus it is the Eightfold Path.
As for all the paths of the various ascetics and brahmins, those of other sects:
"This very Noble Eightfold Path is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent"—thus, among paths, the eightfold is the best.
At the moment of the non-returning path, right view is in the sense of seeing... [and so on]... [up to] right concentration.
Through the state of non-distraction, right concentration causes one to become dispassionate toward the fetters of sensual lust and ill will along with their underlying tendencies,
as well as the underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill will; it causes one to become dispassionate toward the defilements and the aggregates that follow them,
and it causes one to become dispassionate toward all external signs.
Dispassion has dispassion as its object...
[as before] ...Of paths, the eightfold is supreme.
At the moment of the path of arahantship, right view is [right view] in the sense of seeing... [as before] ...

In the sense of non-distraction, right concentration is dispassionate toward lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, and the underlying tendency to ignorance;
it is dispassionate toward the defilements that follow upon those [states] and toward the aggregates;
and it is dispassionate toward all external signs. It is dispassion, having dispassion as its object, having dispassion as its domain, and it has arisen in relation to dispassion.
He stands in dispassion, established in dispassion.
As for "dispassion" (*virāga*):
there are two kinds of dispassion—the Nibbāna that is dispassion, and all those states born of having Nibbāna as their object which are also dispassions; thus they are "dispassions."
The seven factors that arise together proceed toward fading away; thus, fading away is the path.
By means of this path, Buddhas and disciples go to Nibbāna, the direction not yet gone to;
thus, it is the eightfold path.
"Of all the paths belonging to the various sects of recluses and brahmins who hold divergent doctrines,
this very Noble Eightfold Path is the foremost, the best, the preeminent, the supreme, and the most excellent"—
thus, among paths, the eightfold is the best.
Fading away through seeing is right view.
Fading away through directing onto is right intention.
Fading away through grasping is right speech.
Right action is fading away through origination;
right livelihood is fading away through purification;
right effort is fading away through exertion.
The fading away of establishment is right mindfulness.
The fading away of non-distraction is right concentration.
The fading away of establishment is the mindfulness enlightenment factor.
The fading away through investigation is the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena.
The fading away through exertion is the enlightenment factor of energy.
The fading away through pervasion is the enlightenment factor of rapture.
The fading away through tranquility is the factor of enlightenment of serenity.
The fading away through non-distraction is the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
The fading away through reflection is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
The fading away that is unshakable by lack of faith is the power of faith.
The fading away that is unshakable by indolence is the power of energy.
The fading away that is unshakable by negligence is the power of mindfulness.
The fading away through being unshakable by restlessness is the power of concentration.
The fading away through being unshakable by ignorance is the power of wisdom.
The fading away through resolute confidence is the faculty of faith.
Fading away through exertion is the faculty of energy.
Fading away through establishment is the faculty of mindfulness.
Fading away through non-distraction is the faculty of concentration.
Dispassion through vision is the faculty of wisdom.
In the sense of predominance, dispassion is the faculties;
in the sense of unshakability, dispassion is the powers.
In the sense of leading out, the factors of enlightenment are fading away.
In the sense of being the cause, the path is fading away.
In the sense of establishing, the foundations of mindfulness are fading away.
In the sense of striving, the right efforts are fading away.
In the sense of succeeding, the bases of success are fading away.
In the sense of suchness, the truths are fading away.
In the sense of non-distraction, serenity is fading away.
In the sense of contemplation, insight is fading away.
In the sense of a single flavor, serenity and insight together are fading away.
In the sense of non-transgression, the yoke-pair is fading away.
In the sense of restraint, purification of virtue is fading away.
In the sense of non-distraction, purification of mind is fading away.
Purity of view is fading away in the sense of seeing;
liberation is fading away in the sense of being released;
true knowledge is fading away in the sense of penetration.
In the sense of relinquishment, liberation is dispassion.
In the sense of eradication, the knowledge of destruction is dispassion.
Will is dispassion in the sense of being the root.
Volition is fading away in the sense of origination;
contact is fading away in the sense of convergence;
feeling is fading away in the sense of meeting place.
Concentration is fading away in the sense of being preeminent;
mindfulness is fading away in the sense of being sovereign;
wisdom is fading away in the sense of being supreme.
Dispassion (*virāga*) is the path in the sense of liberation;
Nibbāna, which plunges into the deathless, is the path in the sense of the ultimate goal.
Right view is the path of seeing; right intention is the path of directing [the mind] toward [the object]... and so forth.
Nibbāna, which is plunged into the deathless, is the path in the sense of being the ultimate goal.
Thus, dispassion is the path.
How is liberation the fruit?
At the moment of the fruit of stream-entry, right view—in the sense of seeing—is liberated from wrong view;
it is liberated from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it is liberated from all external signs.
This liberation has liberation as its object, has liberation as its domain, is produced by liberation, is established in liberation, and is grounded in liberation.
"Deliverance" means two kinds of deliverance:
Nibbāna itself as deliverance, and all those states born of having Nibbāna as their object which are themselves delivered;
thus, deliverance is the fruit.
In the sense of directing, right intention is liberated from wrong intention;
it is liberated from the defilements that follow upon it and from the aggregates; and it is liberated from all external signs.
Liberation has liberation as its object, has liberation as its domain, has arisen through liberation, stands by means of liberation, and is established in liberation.
"Liberation" means two kinds of liberation:
Nibbāna is liberation, and all those states that have arisen with Nibbāna as their object are liberated;
thus, liberation is the fruit.
In the sense of embracing, right speech is liberated from wrong speech; in the sense of origination, right action is liberated from wrong action;
in the sense of cleansing, right livelihood is liberated from wrong livelihood;
in the sense of exertion, right effort is liberated from wrong effort; in the sense of establishment, right mindfulness is liberated from wrong mindfulness.
Right concentration, in the sense of non-distraction, is liberated from wrong concentration;
it is liberated from the defilements and aggregates that follow upon it; and it is liberated from all external signs.
Liberation has liberation as its object, liberation as its domain, it has arisen through liberation, it is established in liberation, and it is grounded in liberation.
"Liberation" means two kinds of liberation:
Nibbāna is liberation, and all those states that have arisen with Nibbāna as their object are liberated;
thus, liberation is the fruit.
At the moment of the fruit of once-returning, right view in the sense of seeing ... pe ...
right concentration in the sense of non-distraction is liberated from the gross fetters of sensual lust and ill will, from the gross underlying tendencies of sensual lust and ill will;
it is also liberated from the defilements and aggregates that follow upon them, and externally.

And it is liberated from all signs; liberation has liberation as its object, liberation as its domain, it has arisen through liberation, it is established in liberation, and it is grounded in liberation.
"Liberation" refers to two kinds of liberation:
Nibbāna is liberation, and all those states that have arisen with Nibbāna as their object are liberated;
thus, liberation is the fruit.
At the moment of the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), right view in the sense of seeing... [and so on].
In the sense of non-distraction, right concentration is liberated from the fetter of sensual lust and the fetter of ill will, which are accompanied by underlying tendencies;

it is liberated from the underlying tendency to sensual lust and the underlying tendency to ill will that accompany them; it is liberated from the defilements and the aggregates that follow upon them;
and it is liberated from all external signs. This liberation has liberation as its object and has liberation as its domain.
They have emerged through liberation, they stand in liberation, they are established in liberation … [as before] … At the moment of the fruit of arahantship,
right view in the sense of seeing … [as before] … and right concentration in the sense of non-distraction,
[are abandoned] along with lust for the fine-material realm, lust for the immaterial realm, conceit, restlessness, ignorance, and the underlying tendency to conceit.

He is liberated from the underlying tendency toward craving for existence and the underlying tendency toward ignorance; he is liberated from the defilements that follow upon those [tendencies] and from the aggregates;

and he is liberated from all external signs. That liberation has liberation as its object, has liberation as its domain, has arisen through liberation, is established in liberation, and is grounded in liberation.
"Liberation" means two kinds of liberation:
Nibbāna is liberation, and all those states that have arisen with Nibbāna as their object are liberated;
thus, liberation is the fruit.
Liberation through vision is right view …pe… liberation through non-distraction is right concentration;
liberation through establishment is the mindfulness enlightenment factor; liberation through reflection is the equanimity enlightenment factor.
Liberation through unshakability by lack of faith is the power of faith …pe…
The power of wisdom is liberation through unshakability regarding ignorance.
The faculty of faith is liberation through resolute confidence...
[and so on] ...the faculty of wisdom is liberation through vision.
In the sense of predominance, the faculties (*indriya*) are liberation;

in the sense of unshakability, the powers (*bala*) are liberation; in the sense of outlet, the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are liberation; in the sense of cause, the path (*magga*) is liberation;
in the sense of establishment, the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) are liberation; in the sense of exertion, the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*) are liberation; in the sense of success...
The bases of psychic power are liberation in the sense of suchness; the truths are liberation in the sense of suchness; serenity is liberation in the sense of non-distraction;
insight is liberation in the sense of contemplation; serenity and insight are liberation in the sense of single flavor;
the pair is liberation in the sense of non-excess; purification of virtue is liberation in the sense of restraint; purification of mind is liberation in the sense of non-distraction.
In the sense of seeing, purification of view is liberation; in the sense of being liberated, deliverance is liberation;
in the sense of penetration, true knowledge is liberation; in the sense of relinquishment, liberation is liberation; in the sense of subsiding, the knowledge of non-arising is liberation;
in the sense of being the root, desire is liberation; in the sense of origination, attention is liberation; in the sense of convergence, contact is [liberation].

Liberation is liberation in the sense of convergence for feeling; liberation is liberation in the sense of being foremost for concentration; liberation is liberation in the sense of sovereignty for mindfulness;

liberation is liberation in the sense of being supreme for wisdom; liberation is liberation in the sense of being the core; and liberation is liberation in the sense of the final consummation, which is Nibbāna immersed in the deathless.
Thus is the fruit of liberation.
Thus is fading away the path and liberation the fruit.
The discussion on fading away is finished.
